section.title: Divorce, Children, and the Rich Young Man
section.sectionRationale: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus teaches on three matters that test the heart: marriage, which He roots in God's creation design against a culture of easy divorce; children, whom He receives as the very pattern of kingdom entry; and wealth, which grips a sincere seeker so tightly that he turns away from eternal life. Together they show what it means, and what it costs, to receive the kingdom.
section.thesis: The kingdom of God is entered not by achievement or possession but received like a child, so that God's design for marriage is honoured, the lowly are welcomed, and even a moral, wealthy seeker must let go of what he trusts, for what is impossible with man is possible with God.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the teaching on divorce and God's design for marriage; the blessing of the children as the model of receiving the kingdom; and the rich man who cannot let go, with the promise to those who leave all for Jesus.

verses.text: Then Jesus left that place and went into the region of Judea, beyond the Jordan. Again the crowds came to Him and He taught them, as was His custom.
Some Pharisees came to test Him. “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” they inquired.
“What did Moses command you?” He replied.
They answered, “Moses permitted a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away.”
But Jesus told them, “Moses wrote this commandment for you because of your {{sklerokardia|hardness of heart}}.
However, from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’
‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife,
and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh.
Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.”
When they were back inside the house, the disciples asked Jesus about this matter.
So He told them, “Whoever {{apolyo|divorces}} his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her.
And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.”

units.label: Jesus blesses the children
units.note: receive the kingdom like a little child

verses.text: Now people were bringing the little children to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them, and the disciples rebuked those who brought them.
But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little {{paidion|children}} come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”
And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.

units.label: The rich man who could not let go

verses.text: As Jesus started on His way, a man ran up and knelt before Him. “Good Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit {{aionios|eternal}} life?”
“Why do you call Me {{agathos|good}}?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone.
You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not cheat others, honor your father and mother.’”
“Teacher,” he replied, “all these I have kept from my youth.”
Jesus looked at him, loved him, and said to him, “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.”
But the man was saddened by these words and went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.
Then Jesus looked around and said to His disciples, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!”
And the disciples were amazed at His words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God!
It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”
They were even more astonished and said to one another, “Who then can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”
Peter began to say to Him, “Look, we have left everything and followed You.”
“Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “no one who has left home or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for My sake and for the gospel
will fail to receive a hundredfold in the present age, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, along with persecutions, and in the age to come, eternal life.
But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.”

sklerokardia.gloss: Hardness of heart. Jesus says the Mosaic provision for divorce was a concession to human hardness, not God's original design. It names the stubborn, unyielding condition of the fallen heart that God's law regulated but the gospel comes to heal and renew.

apolyo.gloss: To release, send away, divorce. In a culture where a man could dismiss his wife with a certificate, Jesus reasserts the permanence of marriage grounded in creation, so that to divorce and remarry is to break the one-flesh union God has joined.

paidion.gloss: A young child, an infant. Jesus makes the child the pattern of kingdom entry: not because children are innocent achievers but because they receive with empty-handed dependence. The kingdom is welcomed, not earned, like a gift a small child simply receives.

aionios.gloss: Eternal, everlasting, belonging to the age to come. Eternal life is the life of God's kingdom, both a present gift and a future inheritance. The rich man asks how to inherit it, revealing that even the sincere and moral cannot secure it by their own doing.

agathos.gloss: Good. Jesus' question, why do you call Me good, no one is good except God alone, is not a denial of His own goodness but a probe: does the man realize that true goodness belongs to God, and that in calling Jesus good he speaks truer than he knows?

basic.context: As Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, Pharisees test Him on divorce. He points past the Mosaic concession to God's design at creation: one man and one woman joined as one flesh, not to be separated. Then people bring little children, and when the disciples try to shoo them away, Jesus is indignant, insisting the kingdom belongs to such as these and must be received like a child. Next a rich, moral man runs up asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus, loving him, tells him to sell everything and follow, but he goes away sorrowful. Jesus warns how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, that only God can save, and promises abundant reward to all who leave everything for Him.
basic.hermeneutics: The three scenes all probe the heart's true trust. Marriage is grounded in God's creation order, not human convenience. The child models empty-handed dependence, the only way into the kingdom. The rich man shows that even sincere morality cannot save when the heart clings to wealth. The thread is that the kingdom is received as a gift, and receiving it may cost everything.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus traces divorce to sklerokardia, hardness of heart, against God's design; to apolyo, divorce, and remarry breaks the one-flesh union. The kingdom must be received like a paidion, a little child. A man asks how to inherit aionios, eternal, life, and calls Jesus agathos, good, truer than he knows.
basic.typology: God's design of marriage as one flesh points to the union of Christ and His church. The child received into Jesus' arms pictures the way every believer is welcomed. The rich man's failure highlights the treasure in heaven found only in following Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus is the authoritative interpreter of God's law and creation design, the one who welcomes children, and the treasure worth more than all wealth. He looks on the rich man and loves him, even as He calls him to costly discipleship.
basic.god: God designed marriage and joins husband and wife. God receives the lowly and dependent. God alone can save those whom wealth or self-reliance would exclude; with Him the impossible is possible.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1 and 2 ground marriage. Malachi 2 shows God's hatred of faithless divorce. Ephesians 5 unfolds marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.
basic.oneStory: On the way to the cross, Jesus reveals the heart of the kingdom: it cannot be earned, only received like a child. God's good design for marriage, His welcome of the lowly, and His call to let go of every rival treasure all point to the One who gave up everything for us, so that what is impossible for us is made possible by God.

context.literary:
Mark 10:1 to 31 is a three part teaching in a house and on a road, and the common thread is receiving. The first part, 10:1 to 12, deals with a man's hold on a wife, the second, 10:13 to 16, with a child who has nothing to hold, and the third, 10:17 to 31, with a man whose possessions hold him. In each scene a group is shown trying to control access: Pharisees controlling the terms of marriage, disciples controlling who may approach Jesus, and a rich man controlling the terms of eternal life.

The chapter keeps returning to words from chapter 9. The disciples 'hinder' the children, 10:13 to 14, using the same verb as when they tried to stop the exorcist, 9:38 to 39. The verb 'receive' of 9:37 comes back in 10:15. 'First' and 'last' of 9:35 close the passage in 10:31. In this way the teaching on the road continues the lesson on greatness and shows how it plays out in marriage, family and money.

The pattern within each scene is a question followed by Jesus' answer, then a private explanation. The Pharisees ask, and the disciples ask again in the house, 10:10. The rich man asks, and the disciples ask again, 10:26. After Peter's remark, 10:28, Mark closes with the promise that the first will be last. The long answer to the rich man is the most carefully built, with the commandments, the look of love, the five commands of verse 21 and the sorrowful departure all set in a tight sequence.
context.historical:
Jesus is in 'the region of Judea, beyond the Jordan,' the territory ruled by Herod Antipas. Mark has already told us that John the Baptist was arrested for saying it was not lawful for Herod to have his brother's wife, 6:17 to 18. A question about divorce asked here was therefore a trap with political teeth, and Jesus answers it in the place where it had cost John his freedom.

Deuteronomy 24:1 to 4 permits a husband to write a certificate if he found 'some indecency' in his wife. The meaning of that phrase was disputed. Some teachers read it narrowly, as sexual misconduct, and others read it so widely that almost any displeasure qualified. Women in Jewish practice generally had no corresponding right, which is why Mark's mention of a woman divorcing her husband, 10:12, is often taken as an application to the wider Roman world, where it was possible.

In the ancient world a child was weak and dependent, with no rank to bring to a teacher. The rich man's question assumed that wealth was a sign of God's blessing, a view that Proverbs 10:22 and the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy could be made to support. This is why the disciples are 'amazed' in 10:24 and 'even more astonished' in 10:26. The camel was the largest animal the hearers knew, and the eye of a needle the smallest opening; the saying is a deliberate absurdity. The suggestion that 'the needle's eye' was a small gate in Jerusalem has no known ancient support, and it would weaken the point.
context.canonical:
Jesus answers from the first pages of the Bible, quoting Genesis 1:27 and 2:24. He treats the creation account as the standard by which the later concession of Deuteronomy 24 is to be judged, and Malachi 2:13 to 16 already show God grieved by faithless divorce. Paul takes the one flesh union as the pattern for Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31 to 32, and writes of marriage in 1 Corinthians 7:10 to 16, quoting the Lord's command and then addressing cases Jesus had not.

The child saying draws on a line of Old Testament teaching that blesses the humble, from Psalm 131:1 to 2 to Isaiah 66:2, and the Gospel of Luke records the same scene, Luke 18:15 to 17. The picture of Jesus gathering the little ones in His arms fulfils Isaiah 40:11.

The questions about the commandments and eternal life recall Leviticus 18:5, 'the man who does these things will live by them,' and Proverbs 11:28 warns that the one who trusts in his riches will fall. Jesus' answer about treasure in heaven is developed in Matthew 6:19 to 21, and Paul's counsel to the rich, 1 Timothy 6:17 to 19, picks up the same themes. Zacchaeus, Luke 19:1 to 10, shows a rich man who does let go, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house. The promise that nothing is too hard for God goes back to Genesis 18:14 and Job 42:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wants his readers to see that the kingdom has a character, and that it is received in the same way in every area of life. He is not giving a manual on marriage, children and wealth for its own sake. He is showing that the disciples, who had been quarrelling over rank, must still learn what it means to have nothing to offer.

Mark wants those in difficult marriages to understand that God's intention was never failure, and that divorce was a concession to hardness, never a goal. He wants those who are tempted to treat children, women or the poor as less important to see that Jesus does not. And he wants readers who are comfortable to feel the force of the man who walked away. The note that Jesus 'looked at him and loved him' guarantees that the call is not harsh, but the man's sorrow guarantees that it is costly.

The end of the passage was written for those who had left things for Jesus' sake. Peter's remark, 10:28, is answered with a promise that gives and then warns: a hundredfold in this age, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Mark describes what the Pharisees asked, what Moses allowed, and what the man did. What Jesus teaches about God's design for marriage is prescriptive: He bases it on creation and says what God has joined, man should not separate. At the same time the passage does not give a full legal code for every difficult situation, and the church has to use the whole of Scripture, including Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7, to care for those whose marriages have been broken by abuse, desertion or unfaithfulness.

Jesus' command to the rich man is a command to that man, and the lesson is wider than the order. Not every disciple is told to sell everything, since Peter's house at Capernaum and the households that supported the church continued. What is prescriptive is the principle that nothing may stand between a person and Jesus. The hundredfold of verse 30 is a promise of God's family and provision, not a formula for wealth, as the phrase 'with persecutions' makes clear.

debates.question: Is Jesus commanding every believer to sell all their possessions?

views.label: A diagnosis of this man's specific idol
views.case: Jesus, who elsewhere assumes disciples keep homes and help the poor from their means, exposes the one thing gripping this man's heart, his wealth; the command unmasks his true god, showing that following Christ must come first.

views.label: A radical call that may indeed require literal renunciation
views.case: For some, as for this man, discipleship really does demand giving up wealth; the principle that treasure in heaven outweighs earthly riches can require concrete, costly surrender, not merely an inner attitude.

debates.bearing: Both hold that Christ must be supreme over every possession; whether the surrender is literal or of the heart's grip, nothing may rival Him, and only God can free a clutching heart.

debates.question: Why does Jesus respond, why do you call Me good?

views.label: A probe toward His true identity
views.case: Jesus is not disowning goodness but pressing the man to see that if only God is good and Jesus is good, then Jesus is more than a mere teacher; the question invites a deeper recognition of who stands before him.

views.label: An exposure of shallow flattery and self-confidence
views.case: The man's easy compliment and claim to have kept the commandments reveal a superficial view of goodness; Jesus sets the true standard, God alone, to unsettle the man's confidence in his own record.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree Jesus redirects the man from casual moral self-assurance to the searching truth that goodness belongs to God, and that eternal life is God's gift, not a wage.

debates.question: What does it mean to receive the kingdom 'like a little child'?

views.label: Receive it as a child receives it
views.case: The Greek hos paidion can be read either way. The common reading is that the child is the model: empty handed, trusting, unable to earn anything, taking what is given. This fits the next scene, where a man who has kept the commandments from youth cannot receive what he must be given.

views.label: Receive it as you would receive a child
views.case: The saying in 9:37 spoke of welcoming a child in Jesus' name, and the verb 'receive' is the same. On this reading the kingdom is received by those who receive the powerless, and the disciples who turned the children away have shut themselves out.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Mark places the saying between the quarrel about greatness and the rich man, and the scene both honours the child and shows the child's posture. The two meanings are not opposed, since the one who welcomes the lowly is learning to be lowly.

debates.bearing: Whichever grammar is preferred, the point is the same: the kingdom comes as a gift to those who have no claim, and those who cannot bear to be that low will not enter.

debates.question: How do Mark's words on divorce relate to Matthew's exception and to Paul?

views.label: Mark states the principle and Matthew the rule
views.case: Mark gives the creation ideal without qualification, and Matthew 19:9 adds 'except for sexual immorality.' On this view Matthew spells out what was already understood in the debate about Deuteronomy 24, where sexual misconduct was the central ground, and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving partner, 1 Corinthians 7:15.

views.label: Jesus allows no remarriage while the first spouse lives
views.case: Others, including a long strand of early church teaching, hold that the saying forbids remarriage in all cases, treating the Matthean clause as describing a separation, not a dissolution. They point to Paul's own command that a separated wife stay unmarried or be reconciled, 1 Corinthians 7:10 to 11.

views.label: A prophetic ideal addressed to those who abused the concession
views.case: Others note that Jesus is answering men who treated divorce as a right, and that the saying is aimed at the practice of discarding wives for new ones. On this reading the text is principally a protection for the one divorced, and it calls for mercy as well as discipline in how the church handles broken marriages.

debates.bearing: All three views hold that marriage is the work of God and not a contract to be ended for convenience, and that divorce is always a sign of hardened hearts. They differ over how that principle is applied to particular cases, and this study does not try to settle them. Churches should handle these questions with both the strictness of Jesus' words and the mercy of His welcome.

study.originalLanguages:
The union of marriage is described with two verbs Mark records in Jesus' words. The man 'will be united' to his wife, proskollao, a word that means to be glued or joined fast, and in 10:9 God 'has joined together,' syzeugnymi, the word for yoking two animals under one harness. The second verb is the sort of word a farmer would use. What God has yoked, human beings are told not to chorizo, to split apart, using a present command, 'let man not separate.'

The Pharisees mention a 'certificate of divorce,' in Greek biblion apostasiou, which is the phrase of the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 24:1. Jesus does not argue with the wording; he moves behind it. Verse 11 says a man who divorces and remarries commits adultery 'against her,' epi with the accusative, and so makes the first wife the one wronged. That is often noted as unusual in a world where adultery was thought of as a wrong done to a husband, not a wife, and it gives the wife a standing before God.

When the disciples turn the children away, Jesus is 'indignant,' aganakteo, the same verb used of the ten who are angry with James and John in 10:41. He tells them not to 'hinder,' koluo, which is the verb of 9:38 to 39 when the disciples stopped the unauthorised exorcist. The kingdom must be 'received,' dechomai, as in 9:37. Jesus takes the children in His arms, enankalizomai, and blesses them, and Mark uses the same verb of the child in 9:36.

The rich man asks what to do 'to inherit' eternal life, kleronomeo. Inheritance is not earned; it is given, and the man's own verb undermines his question. Jesus 'looked at him and loved him,' emblepo and agapao. Then come five imperatives in verse 21, hypage, poleson, dos, deuro, akolouthei, go, sell, give, come, follow, so that four of them clear the way and one is the point. The man leaves 'saddened,' stygnazo, a word used elsewhere of a darkened or lowering sky, so his face is clouded.

The astonished disciples ask who can be saved, and Jesus uses a contrast, adynaton and dynata, impossible and possible. The same adjective, dynata, appears when Jesus says all things are possible to the one who believes, 9:23, and when He prays to His Father, 14:36. And the promise of verse 30 carries the phrase 'with persecutions,' meta diogmon, a phrase that Matthew and Luke leave out.

typology.type: Adam and Eve, one flesh, Genesis 2:24
typology.fulfillment: The first marriage is the pattern for every marriage, because God Himself brought the woman to the man, Genesis 2:22. Paul quotes the verse and says 'this mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:31 to 32. The correspondence is that Christ leaves His Father's side for the sake of His bride, as the husband leaves father and mother, and is joined to her in a union that is not to be dissolved. The escalation is that Christ gives Himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25, so that human marriage is a picture of a love that cost a life. The type falls short because earthly marriage ends in death, Romans 7:2, and the union with Christ does not.

typology.type: The hard heart and the heart of flesh, Ezekiel 36:26
typology.fulfillment: Jesus says the Mosaic concession came because of hardness of heart, 10:5. The prophets answer that problem with a promise: 'I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh,' Ezekiel 36:26, and God will write His law on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33. The correspondence is between the hard heart that required a concession and the new heart that does not. Its fulfilment is in the new covenant that Jesus will seal, Mark 14:24, in which the Spirit gives power to live what the creation order requires. The type falls short in that the hard heart still lingers in believers, and so the church needs both the ideal and the mercy of repentance.

typology.type: The shepherd who gathers lambs in His arms, Isaiah 40:11
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah says the LORD 'gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart.' In Mark 10:16 Jesus does exactly what God was said to do for the weakest of His flock. The disciples see an interruption, and Jesus acts as the Shepherd of Israel. The correspondence is not a hidden code but an acted portrait, and it is one of the places where Jesus does what the prophets said God would do. The escalation is that He lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The type falls short only in that a picture of care is not yet the full price of rescue.

God told Abram to leave his country, kindred and father's household and go to a land that would be shown. Peter's claim in 10:28, 'we have left everything,' and Jesus' promise of a hundredfold, 10:29 to 30, belong to the same pattern: leaving the secure for the sake of God's word and receiving more than was given up. The rich man's refusal is the opposite of Abraham's obedience. The escalation is that the one who calls is Jesus Himself and the reward is eternal life. Hebrews 11:8 to 10 shows that the land was itself a pointer to a city, and the type falls short because Abraham's inheritance was a promise held at a distance.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by His authority. When asked about Moses, Jesus does not pick a side between the schools but goes to Genesis and speaks with the confidence of One who knows the Creator's mind. He sets Moses' provision beside God's original word and treats the original as final, and He does not need to cite a rabbi. That is the posture of the Son, who in Hebrews is the one through whom the universe was made, Hebrews 1:2.

It leads to Christ by His compassion. He is 'indignant' on the children's behalf, takes them in His arms and blesses them. In the next scene He 'looked at him and loved him,' even though the man would walk away. The same Jesus who is stern about divorce and wealth is tender to those who come to Him empty. Jesus' love for the man did not lead Him to soften the demand, and His demand did not lead Him to withdraw His love.

It leads to Christ by contrast and exchange. The man had great wealth and was saddened; Christ, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, and does so gladly. Jesus says the rich man lacks one thing and then invites him to come and follow, which means that the one thing the man lacks is Jesus. The treasure in heaven is not an abstract reward, for to follow Him is to be where He is.

It leads to Christ by the impossible made possible. 'Who then can be saved?' asks the amazed crowd. The answer is not a technique but a person: salvation is possible with God, and the Gospel will go on to show how, in the death of the Son of Man as a ransom, 10:45. The one who tells the rich man to give everything away will Himself give all, Philippians 2:6 to 8.

A caution: the child in Jesus' arms is not a symbol of Christ, and the rich man is not an allegory. The links rest on what Jesus does and says in the passage and on how the New Testament explains it.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the maker with a purpose. Jesus appeals to what God made 'from the beginning of creation,' and the verb 'joined' makes God the active party in every marriage that is rightly made. Marriage is not a human invention that God later tolerated. It is His design, and the design carries moral weight, since to break what He has joined is to act against Him.

It shows a God who welcomes the helpless. The disciples assume that God's attention goes to the important, and Jesus corrects them with indignation. The kingdom belongs to such as these, and the Father who gives it gives it as a gift. This is not sentimentality. It is the logic of grace, in which the one who cannot repay is the one who receives.

It shows God as the only standard of goodness. 'No one is good except God alone' is not a denial that Jesus is good, but a statement about where goodness is found. Every measure of human righteousness, including keeping the commandments from youth, is measured against Him. At the same time the verse echoes the confession that the LORD is one, Deuteronomy 6:4, and it presses the man toward the answer that the one he addresses as 'Good Teacher' is more than a teacher.

God's love is shown to be searching and not sentimental. Jesus loves the man and still names what holds him. Love does not lower the price; it states it plainly.

God is also the one who does the impossible. 'All things are possible with God' recalls Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' and Job's confession that God can do all things, Job 42:2. The camel and the needle show that the human problem is beyond human repair, and the answer is not better effort but divine action. Salvation begins and ends with God.

For worship, the passage invites us to come as children, with open hands, and to let Him be the one who gives, who joins, who loves and who saves.

crossReferences.note: Jesus quotes the creation of humanity as male and female to show what God intended before any concession was needed. The verse establishes that marriage rests on how God made people, and so the argument about divorce is carried back past Moses to the beginning.

The statement that a man leaves father and mother and is united to his wife, becoming one flesh, is the text on which Jesus builds the whole answer. Because the union is made by God and creates a new unit, it cannot be treated as an ordinary contract that either side may end at will.

The passage Moses wrote, which the Pharisees cite, gives the procedure for a certificate of divorce. Jesus reads it as regulation of an existing evil, a concession to hardness of heart, not as a statement of what God desired, which fits the way the law restrains harm without endorsing it.

The LORD says that He hates divorce and that the one who breaks faith with the wife of his youth covers his garment with violence. The prophet shows that God has always cared about the person wronged by a broken marriage, which is the same concern in Mark 10:11.

The parallel account adds the phrase 'except for sexual immorality' and the disciples' reaction that it is better not to marry. Reading the two Gospels together shows that Mark records the central principle and Matthew records the way it was applied in the debate.

Paul quotes the same verse of Genesis and says it is a profound mystery that refers to Christ and the church. The one flesh union is therefore both a created pattern for marriage and a picture of the love Christ has for His people, which is why it must not be broken lightly.

God is pictured as a shepherd who gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. When Jesus takes the children in His arms in Mark 10:16, He does for them what Isaiah said God Himself would do, and the disciples' rebuke is shown to be against the heart of God.

Zacchaeus is a rich man who gives half his possessions to the poor and repays fourfold, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house. The two stories show that wealth is not the barrier in itself, and that what matters is whether the heart is free to let it go.

Paul tells the rich not to be conceited or to hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but to set their hope on God and to be generous. The counsel works out what Jesus meant in practice for those who keep possessions, and it matches the invitation to store up treasure in heaven.

God asks whether anything is too difficult for the LORD when Sarah laughs at the promise of a son. The question lies behind Jesus' answer in Mark 10:27, because in both cases the impossible human situation becomes the place where God's power is shown.

Paul describes Christ as rich and becoming poor so that others might become rich. It stands beside the rich man's story as its answer: the one who asks the man to give up everything is the one who gave up everything first.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a garden in which a man and a woman are joined by God and given everything but one tree. The fall that follows is a failure of receiving, a grasping of what was not given, and the history that follows shows hearts that have hardened and a world in which marriages break, the weak are pushed aside and wealth becomes a god. Jesus' answers in this chapter are answers to the whole of that story.

By going back to Genesis He shows that God's purpose for marriage has not changed and that the law's concessions were provisional. By welcoming the children He shows what the people of God look like: those who take what is given. And by saying that the rich man lacks one thing, He puts His finger on the oldest human problem, the wish to secure our own life by what we hold. The first man refused to depend on God and reached; the rich man, offered a place with Jesus, holds on.

The passage also points to the way out of the story. The one who asks the man to leave everything will do so Himself. The disciples have left their nets, and Jesus promises a family that includes mothers, children and fields in the present age, so that the people of God are a household in which what is lost is restored, with persecutions and with eternal life at the end. Marriage, children and wealth all appear again in the final chapters of the Bible, where the church is the bride, the saved are His children, and the city is pure gold, Revelation 21:2 to 7 and 21:18.

The new creation fulfils the promise of verse 30. Those who have given up what they could not keep receive what they could not earn: 'the first will be last, and the last will be first' is turned into a world where the humble inherit, Matthew 5:5, and the covenant of marriage between Christ and His people is finally celebrated, Revelation 19:7.

quiz.q: How does Jesus answer the question about divorce?

options.text: He points past Moses' concession to God's creation design: one man and one woman joined as one flesh, not to be separated.
options.note: Mark 10:5-9; Jesus grounds marriage in creation, calling the Mosaic permission a concession to hard hearts.

options.text: He says Moses' certificate of divorce settles the matter.
options.note: Jesus says that provision was for hardness of heart, not God's original intent.

options.text: He upholds the permanence of marriage while acknowledging human sin.
options.note: True in substance, but it should name the creation ground: what God has joined, let no one separate.

options.text: He declares that marriage does not matter to God.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus stresses that God joins and honours marriage.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus say the kingdom must be received like a little child?

options.text: Because it is received with empty-handed dependence, as a gift, not earned by achievement.
options.note: Mark 10:15; entry is by childlike reception, not merit.

options.text: Because children are morally innocent and sinless.
options.note: The point is dependence and reception, not a claim of childhood innocence.

options.text: Because the humble and lowly are welcomed by God.
options.note: True and related, but the specific lesson is receiving the kingdom with a child's empty-handed trust.

options.text: Because children can earn God's favour more easily.
options.note: No one earns the kingdom; it is received as a gift, which is the whole point.

quiz.q: Why did the rich man go away sorrowful?

options.text: He would not surrender the wealth his heart clung to, though Jesus, loving him, called him to follow.
options.note: Mark 10:21-22; his great wealth held him back from following Jesus.

options.text: Because Jesus told him he had not kept the commandments.
options.note: The man claimed to have kept them; his failure was the idol of wealth Jesus exposed.

options.text: Because he was unwilling to part with what he trusted more than Christ.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should note Jesus' love for him and the specific call to sell all and follow.

options.text: Because Jesus refused to give him eternal life.
options.note: Jesus lovingly showed him the way; the man turned away himself.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean that with God the impossible is possible for salvation?

options.text: No one, rich or otherwise, can save themselves, but God can save even those bound by wealth or self-reliance.
options.note: Mark 10:27; salvation is God's work, possible with Him though impossible for man.

options.text: That rich people simply need to try harder to enter the kingdom.
options.note: The opposite; human effort cannot achieve it, which is why only God can save.

options.text: That God can rescue those whom human effort cannot save.
options.note: True, but it should include that this applies to everyone, since with man salvation is impossible.

options.text: That salvation is possible only for the poor.
options.note: The rich can be saved too, but only by God's power, not by their own doing.

quiz.q: What does Jesus promise those who leave everything for Him and the gospel?

options.text: A hundredfold now, homes and family and fields along with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come.
options.note: Mark 10:29-30 pairs abundant present reward, including persecutions, with future eternal life.

options.text: A hundredfold of homes, family, and fields in this present age.
options.note: True but partial; Jesus adds along with persecutions and eternal life in the age to come.

options.text: A trouble-free life of comfort and prosperity.
options.note: Jesus explicitly includes persecutions; the reward is not a comfortable life.

options.text: Nothing in this life, only reward after death.
options.note: Jesus promises a hundredfold in the present age as well as eternal life to come.

questions: Jesus rooted marriage in God's creation design rather than human convenience. How does seeing marriage as something God joins shape the way you view commitment and faithfulness?
Jesus welcomed the children the disciples tried to turn away. Who are the overlooked people you might be tempted to hinder from coming to Jesus?
The kingdom must be received like a child, with empty hands. Where are you still trying to earn what God gives only as a gift?
Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him, yet named the one thing he could not release. What is the one thing your heart most struggles to surrender to Christ?
Jesus promised abundant reward, with persecutions, to those who leave all for Him. How does that honest promise reshape what you expect from following Jesus?

translationNotes.note: And if a woman divorces her husband reflects a setting where, unlike strict Jewish custom, a wife might initiate divorce; Jesus applies the same standard to both, an unusually even-handed word for the time.
Some manuscripts add take up the cross after come, follow Me, echoing Mark 8:34; either way the call is to wholehearted, costly discipleship.
Some manuscripts read how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter, interpreting Jesus' point: the peril is not wealth itself but trusting in it rather than in God.
